alternatives.label: Saudi East-West pipeline to Yanbu (Red Sea) plus UAE Abu Dhabi-Fujairah pipeline
alternatives.note: Stated capacities in the atlas's pipeline layer: Saudi East-West (Petroline) 7,000 kb/d; ADCOP (Habshan-Fujairah) 1,500 kb/d (Wikipedia, 2026). Goreh-Jask (Iran) about 0.3 mb/d effective; a planned UAE Jebel Dhanna-Fujairah line of 1.5 mb/d by 2027. Yanbu route depends on Red Sea security.

summary: The only sea exit from the Persian Gulf, carrying about a fifth of world oil consumption and roughly a fifth of global LNG trade in 2024. Since the US-Israeli strikes on Iran on 28 February 2026 it has been largely closed to commercial traffic, the largest oil supply disruption on record.

tanker.name: tanker
tanker.line: Tanker: 'at least' 828 Mt is 90% of IMF PortWatch's 915 Mt for all tanker ships in 2024; the ports or routes the atlas assumes may overstate the passage.
tanker.n: IMF PortWatch's volume is an estimate made from ship movements (915 Mt in 2024; 1,056 Mt in 2022, its best full year since 2019), and the atlas's groups are not all the cargo these ships carry, so an 'at least' tonnage this close to it leaves little room: the ports or routes the atlas assumes may overstate the passage. The 'up to' figure of a group cannot exceed the whole of PortWatch's volume of these ships (915 Mt), and is not reduced by the other groups' 'at least' tonnage, because the atlas's own tonnage is above 85% of that volume and the two are too close to compare. The cap binds only where a figure is tagged 'capped at PortWatch volume': none of the 8 tanker groups with an estimate at this passage

traffic.n: Tankers, dry bulk, container, general cargo and ro-ro (IMF PortWatch daily transits); 2023 average 92.3/day; 2025 average 85.5/day

trafficVol.n: Estimated trade volume of the vessels counted (IMF PortWatch estimate, not a customs statistic); 2023 average 3.69 Mt/day; 2025 average 3.22 Mt/day

name: Strait of Malacca
limits: Shallow sections constrain the largest tankers. Wikipedia (Malaccamax, 2026) gives the strait as 25 m deep and a typical Malaccamax tanker, the largest that can pass it, as up to 333 m long and 60 m wide with a 20.5 m draught and 300,000 dwt; not stated in the EIA page.

name: Lombok Strait
limits: Deep water suitable for fully laden Capesize and VLCC vessels; Wikipedia (Lombok Strait, 2026) gives a depth of about 250 m.
summary: Deep-water route between Bali and Lombok used by Capesizes and VLCCs too deep for Malacca, and an alternative if Malacca is restricted. Preferred for Australian iron ore and coal to north Asia.
parallelNote: Ships can also take the Alas Strait, between Lombok and Sumbawa, about 50 nm longer on the Port Hedland to Qingdao run; the atlas counts them at Lombok.

dry.name: dry bulk
dry.line: Dry bulk: 'at least' 850 Mt is 89% of IMF PortWatch's 950 Mt for all dry bulk ships in 2024; the ports or routes the atlas assumes may overstate the passage.
dry.n: IMF PortWatch's volume is an estimate made from ship movements (950 Mt in 2024; 1,025 Mt in 2025, its best full year since 2019), and the atlas's groups are not all the cargo these ships carry, so an 'at least' tonnage this close to it leaves little room: the ports or routes the atlas assumes may overstate the passage. The 'up to' figure of a group cannot exceed the whole of PortWatch's volume of these ships (950 Mt), and is not reduced by the other groups' 'at least' tonnage, because the atlas's own tonnage is above 85% of that volume and the two are too close to compare. The cap binds only where a figure is tagged 'capped at PortWatch volume': 1 of the 27 dry bulk groups with an estimate at this passage

traffic.n: Tankers, dry bulk, container, general cargo and ro-ro (IMF PortWatch daily transits); 2023 average 37.5/day; 2025 average 35.8/day

trafficVol.n: Estimated trade volume of the vessels counted (IMF PortWatch estimate, not a customs statistic); 2023 average 2.66 Mt/day; 2025 average 2.96 Mt/day

dry.line: Dry bulk: 'at least' 312 Mt, above IMF PortWatch's 184 Mt for all dry bulk ships in 2024; the atlas routes cargo on the normal itinerary, so this is the tonnage of the normal route, not the 2024 traffic.
dry.n: IMF PortWatch's volume is an estimate made from ship movements (184 Mt in 2024; 380 Mt in 2023, its best full year since 2019), and the atlas's groups are not all the cargo these ships carry. The atlas routes cargo on the normal itinerary, so this is the tonnage of the normal route, not the 2024 traffic. The atlas's alert "Red Sea diversions" says: "Since Houthi attacks on merchant ships near Bab el-Mandeb began on 19 November 2023, hundreds of commercial vessels, container ships above all, have sailed around the Cape of Good Hope instead of through the Red Sea and the Suez Canal" (Wikipedia, Red Sea crisis). The 'up to' figures of these groups are not capped at PortWatch's volume here: they are tonnages of the normal route, and the 2024 traffic is not a ceiling for them

detour.n: Volume-weighted median over 144 mapped lanes that use this passage, at each lane's typical laden speed

traffic.n: Tankers, dry bulk, container, general cargo and ro-ro (IMF PortWatch daily transits); 2023 average 73.7/day; 2025 average 38.5/day

trafficVol.n: Estimated trade volume of the vessels counted (IMF PortWatch estimate, not a customs statistic); 2023 average 3.35 Mt/day; 2025 average 1.39 Mt/day

name: Bab el-Mandeb
limits: About 18 miles wide at the narrowest point, with the shipping lanes in the Perim channel; no draft limit for oil tankers.

f.n: EIA via Rigzone

alternatives.label: Cape of Good Hope
alternatives.note: Main alternative; no pipeline bypass listed by EIA.

summary: Southern entrance to the Red Sea, connecting Suez to the Indian Ocean. Targeted by Houthi attacks since November 2023 and again by the Houthi blockade of Saudi Arabia in 2026; now also carrying Saudi bypass crude from Yanbu.

dry.name: dry bulk
dry.line: Dry bulk: 'at least' 301 Mt, above IMF PortWatch's 177 Mt for all dry bulk ships in 2024; the atlas routes cargo on the normal itinerary, so this is the tonnage of the normal route, not the 2024 traffic.
dry.n: IMF PortWatch's volume is an estimate made from ship movements (177 Mt in 2024; 381 Mt in 2023, its best full year since 2019), and the atlas's groups are not all the cargo these ships carry. The atlas routes cargo on the normal itinerary, so this is the tonnage of the normal route, not the 2024 traffic. The atlas's alert "Red Sea diversions" says: "Since Houthi attacks on merchant ships near Bab el-Mandeb began on 19 November 2023, hundreds of commercial vessels, container ships above all, have sailed around the Cape of Good Hope instead of through the Red Sea and the Suez Canal" (Wikipedia, Red Sea crisis). The 'up to' figures of these groups are not capped at PortWatch's volume here: they are tonnages of the normal route, and the 2024 traffic is not a ceiling for them

traffic.n: Tankers, dry bulk, container, general cargo and ro-ro (IMF PortWatch daily transits); 2023 average 74.0/day; 2025 average 33.5/day

trafficVol.n: Estimated trade volume of the vessels counted (IMF PortWatch estimate, not a customs statistic); 2023 average 3.37 Mt/day; 2025 average 1.20 Mt/day

name: Panama Canal
limits: Two lock systems: Panamax (about 32.3 m beam) and Neopanamax (since 2016, larger LNG and LPG carriers). Draft and slot limits vary with Gatun Lake levels.

trafficRef.n: Fiscal year ending 30 Sep 2025; 3,342 Neopanamax, 10,062 Panamax

summary: Connects Atlantic and Pacific, key for US Gulf LPG, grain and products to Asia and west-coast South America, and for containers. Drought in 2023-24 limited transits; FY2025 transits recovered to 13,404.

tanker.line: Tanker: 'at least' 104 Mt is 97% of IMF PortWatch's 107 Mt for all tanker ships in 2024; the ports or routes the atlas assumes may overstate the passage.
tanker.n: IMF PortWatch's volume is an estimate made from ship movements (107 Mt in 2024; 122 Mt in 2022, its best full year since 2019), and the atlas's groups are not all the cargo these ships carry, so an 'at least' tonnage this close to it leaves little room: the ports or routes the atlas assumes may overstate the passage. The 'up to' figure of a group cannot exceed the whole of PortWatch's volume of these ships (107 Mt), and is not reduced by the other groups' 'at least' tonnage, because the atlas's own tonnage is above 85% of that volume and the two are too close to compare. The cap binds only where a figure is tagged 'capped at PortWatch volume': none of the 7 tanker groups with an estimate at this passage

dry.line: Dry bulk: 'at least' 207 Mt, above IMF PortWatch's 203 Mt for all dry bulk ships in 2024; the ports, routes or ship types the atlas assumes probably overstate the passage.
dry.n: IMF PortWatch's volume is an estimate made from ship movements (203 Mt in 2024; 241 Mt in 2021, its best full year since 2019), and the atlas's groups are not all the cargo these ships carry, so a tonnage of the atlas above it, with no alert that explains it, means that the ports, routes or ship types the atlas assumes probably overstate the passage. The 'up to' figure of a group cannot exceed the whole of PortWatch's volume of these ships (203 Mt), and is not reduced by the other groups' 'at least' tonnage, because the atlas's own tonnage is above 85% of that volume and the two are too close to compare. The cap binds only where a figure is tagged 'capped at PortWatch volume': none of the 31 dry bulk groups with an estimate at this passage

trafficVol.n: Estimated trade volume of the vessels counted (IMF PortWatch estimate, not a customs statistic); 2023 average 1.14 Mt/day; 2025 average 1.16 Mt/day

name: Danish Straits
portwatchNote: IMF PortWatch counts the Oresund only. It has no counter for the Great Belt, the other main passage of the Danish Straits, so this series is not the traffic of the Danish Straits as a whole.
limits: Shallow, draft-restricted passages in the Great Belt and Oresund. Wikipedia (Drogden, 2026) gives the Drogden channel (Oresund) a depth of about 8 m for passing ships; this is a channel depth, not an official draught limit. No Great Belt figure is given in the sources the atlas uses.

dry.name: dry bulk
dry.line: Dry bulk: 'at least' 394 Mt, above IMF PortWatch's 384 Mt for all dry bulk ships in 2024; the ports, routes or ship types the atlas assumes probably overstate the passage.
dry.n: IMF PortWatch's volume is an estimate made from ship movements (384 Mt in 2024; 514 Mt in 2023, its best full year since 2019), and the atlas's groups are not all the cargo these ships carry, so a tonnage of the atlas above it, with no alert that explains it, means that the ports, routes or ship types the atlas assumes probably overstate the passage. The 'up to' figure of a group cannot exceed the whole of PortWatch's volume of these ships (384 Mt), and is not reduced by the other groups' 'at least' tonnage, because the atlas's own tonnage is above 85% of that volume and the two are too close to compare. The cap binds only where a figure is tagged 'capped at PortWatch volume': none of the 38 dry bulk groups with an estimate at this passage

traffic.n: Tankers, dry bulk, container, general cargo and ro-ro (IMF PortWatch daily transits); 2023 average 146.4/day; 2025 average 135.4/day

trafficVol.n: Estimated trade volume of the vessels counted (IMF PortWatch estimate, not a customs statistic); 2023 average 4.11 Mt/day; 2025 average 3.54 Mt/day

name: Dover Strait
limits: Deep-draft route (the Dover Strait traffic separation scheme); the strait is about 20 m deep over its highest banks and 68 m in its deepest part (Wikipedia, Strait of Dover, 2026).
summary: Busiest strait in the world by transits, linking the North Sea to the English Channel for ARA and Baltic traffic.
parallelNote: Ships can also reach the North Sea north of Scotland, about 160 nm longer from Corpus Christi to Rotterdam; the atlas counts them at Dover.

dry.name: dry bulk
dry.line: Dry bulk: 'at least' 1,016 Mt is 93% of IMF PortWatch's 1,085 Mt for all dry bulk ships in 2024; the ports or routes the atlas assumes may overstate the passage.
dry.n: IMF PortWatch's volume is an estimate made from ship movements (1,085 Mt in 2024; 1,124 Mt in 2023, its best full year since 2019), and the atlas's groups are not all the cargo these ships carry, so an 'at least' tonnage this close to it leaves little room: the ports or routes the atlas assumes may overstate the passage. The 'up to' figure of a group cannot exceed the whole of PortWatch's volume of these ships (1,085 Mt), and is not reduced by the other groups' 'at least' tonnage, because the atlas's own tonnage is above 85% of that volume and the two are too close to compare. The cap binds only where a figure is tagged 'capped at PortWatch volume': 1 of the 22 dry bulk groups with an estimate at this passage

tanker.name: tanker
tanker.line: Tanker: 'at least' 13.6 Mt, above IMF PortWatch's 13.5 Mt for all tanker ships in 2024; the ports, routes or ship types the atlas assumes probably overstate the passage.
tanker.n: IMF PortWatch's volume is an estimate made from ship movements (13.5 Mt in 2024; 14.4 Mt in 2023, its best full year since 2019), and the atlas's groups are not all the cargo these ships carry, so a tonnage of the atlas above it, with no alert that explains it, means that the ports, routes or ship types the atlas assumes probably overstate the passage. The 'up to' figure of a group cannot exceed the whole of PortWatch's volume of these ships (13.5 Mt), and is not reduced by the other groups' 'at least' tonnage, because the atlas's own tonnage is above 85% of that volume and the two are too close to compare. The cap binds only where a figure is tagged 'capped at PortWatch volume': 2 of the 5 tanker groups with an estimate at this passage
